content.thinking:
I'm starting on the postmortem and keeping the symptom short: shop pages responded slowly, so I'll pick a plain active verb and skip any number for now. The causal chain opens with shop requests becoming slow, since the p95 latency series rose above its line, citing AL1 and T6.

Next I'm working through the causal chain: the CPU hit its limit, so requests waited, and the trigger was a rise in request volume against fixed capacity, with deploys and flag changes ruled out. I'm also checking whether the load reached that limit because each request costs more CPU than it should.

I'm settling on the root cause: request volume rose against a fixed CPU limit and a fixed replica count, and nothing added capacity as the load grew, so the CPU saturated and requests queued. The autoscaling gap reads as a contributing safeguard rather than the cause itself. I'm also starting the first step, a symptom line about shop requests slowing and the slowest ones taking far longer than usual from onset.

Now I'm laying out the remaining steps: the service couldn't add capacity on its own with three replicas and a fixed CPU limit, and I'm noting that adding replicas is what ended the incident, though that stays in the document rather than this step.

I'm settling the contributing factors now: the replica count never grew with the load, since no autoscaling showed up and the replicas stayed at the same number until someone scaled out by hand. Had capacity been added as the load climbed, the saturation would have been shorter or might not have happened at all.

I'm moving on to the contributing factors now: the replica count never grew with the load and no autoscaling showed up, and I'm noting the manual scale-out as a mitigation rather than a prevention. Next I'm looking at the default account page doing extra per-request work, which likely pushed each request's CPU cost up and reached the limit sooner, though that rests on an unrun reading. Last, nobody was paged because the alert doesn't page, and I'm treating that as a condition that existed before the incident started.

I'm turning to the detection side now: the alert pages on the p95 latency, and it only fires after a five-minute wait, while nothing alerts on CPU nearing its limit.

I'm weighing whether a CPU-headroom alert would have caught the saturation earlier, but the record doesn't show CPU climbing before onset, so I'll leave that as speculation and not add it as a factor.

Now I'm drafting the action items, starting with a prevention step to set CPU-based autoscaling on the shop deployment so the replicas grow with request volume, which answers the missing-capacity factor.

Next I'm adding a prevention item to page an on-call person when the high-latency alert fires on the shop service, and a second to rework the per-item spend logic before the flag is widened. Neither of these answers a contributing factor yet, so I'm leaving that field empty.

I'm going through what went well: Argus scaled out io-shop to mitigate the incident, checked the flag provider's history itself before acting to rule out flag changes, and the Code-Fix Agent proposed a draft pull request. I'm also noting that the Mitigation Agent waited and confirmed against the metrics before declaring it mitigated. For what went wrong, I'm only settling on one point: nobody was paged.

I'm checking whether the error rate or the takings moved, and they didn't really change, so the impact stays with the latency. I'm also noting the assumptions: that requests queued for CPU is inferred from saturation alongside latency rather than measured, that the CPU limit was fixed, and that the per-request cost reading was never run. I'm drafting the cause in plain words: far more shopper requests arrived than usual, and the shop's servers had a fixed amount of computing power that this load used up, so requests had to wait.

I'm working out the root cause in plain terms: request volume to io-shop rose well above its earlier level while CPU capacity stayed fixed, so the CPU hit its limit and requests queued behind it. I'm also noting that the account page likely does more work per request than it needs, which would have brought the limit on sooner.

I'm settling on the symptom line now: shop pages responded slowly, with no number yet. The first link in the chain is that people using the shop waited much longer for responses, with the slowest requests taking far longer than usual.

I'm working out the chain's second and third steps: the slowest requests kept climbing above their usual level from the onset, and I'm ruling out deploys and flag changes as causes. Then I'm turning to the step about the fixed CPU allowance that the higher request volume outgrew.

I'm checking the counterfactual for each contributing factor: had replicas been added as volume climbed, CPU would likely never have reached its limit. For the account page's per-request cost, the same rise in volume would probably have stayed under the limit or hit it later, which is what the per-item spend fix is meant to address.

I'm deciding to avoid the PR number and just refer to the draft pull request by its role instead.

action_items.item: Set up CPU-based autoscaling for the io-shop deployment so that its replica count grows with request volume before CPU reaches its limit.
Route the HighLatency alert on io-shop to an on-call person so that someone is paged when it fires.
Rework typical_spend_per_item in src/io_shop/typical_spend.py, which Code-Fix's reading describes as quadratic, before the typical-purchase rollout flag is widened.

causal_chain.step: People using the shop waited much longer for responses: from the onset, the response time that nearly all requests stay under climbed far above its usual level, and the latency alert fired.
Requests were waiting for CPU: the service's CPU use rose to the limit set for it and stayed close to that limit while the service was broken.

ruled_out.what: A deploy, release or flag change on io-shop: no production changes came back for the day before the onset.
A flag change made by anyone other than Argus: the flag provider's history showed none in the hour before it was read.

causal_chain.step: The CPU filled up because request volume climbed far above its earlier level. Nothing about the service changed: the change that set the incident off was the rise in load.
The higher volume outgrew the fixed CPU that the service's {T7.2} replicas had as of T7.

input.cause_in_plain_words: Far more requests than usual reached the shop and used up the fixed amount of computing power its servers had, so requests had to wait their turn; the shop's account page likely also does much more work per request than it needs to, which made that limit come sooner.

contributing_factors.factor: The service did not add replicas as load grew. It stayed at {T7.2} replicas (as of T7) until the Mitigation Agent scaled it out by hand. No autoscaling of io-shop was seen in the record.
contributing_factors.had_it_been_otherwise: Replicas would have been added as request volume climbed, before CPU reached its limit. Requests would not have queued, or the slow stretch would have been shorter.
contributing_factors.label: CF-1

contributing_factors.factor: According to Code-Fix's reading of src/io_shop/spend_summary.py, the account page's default path (when neither rollout flag is set) likely re-adds a shopper's whole purchase history once for every purchase on each render. That would make each request cost far more CPU than its answer needs. Nothing ran this reading.
contributing_factors.had_it_been_otherwise: Each request would likely have cost much less CPU, so the same rise in volume would have reached the CPU limit later or not at all.
contributing_factors.label: CF-2

went_well.item: Argus read the flag provider's history itself before acting and found no flag changes by anyone else.
The Mitigation Agent scaled out the io-shop deployment for C1.
The Mitigation Agent checked the service against its metrics before judging the action confirmed, rather than assuming the scale-out had worked.
The Code-Fix Agent proposed a fix as a draft pull request for a person to review.

went_wrong: Nobody was paged: no on-call incident was linked to the alert, so no person was brought in when it fired.

input.root_cause: Request volume to io-shop rose well above its earlier level while the service ran on a fixed amount of CPU ({T7.2} replicas, each under a CPU limit, as of T7). CPU use climbed to that limit, so requests had to wait for CPU and response times stretched.
input.still_at_risk: Another rise in request volume could use up the service's CPU again and slow its responses the same way.
